samples.summary: The guard's coverage is enforced by a hand-written controller list, so a seventh v1 controller ships ungated with CI green
samples.evidence: The guard is bound per controller (`@UseGuards(CombinedAuthGuard, WorkspaceScopeGuard, ApiKeyWriteScopeGuard)` repeated in all six files) rather than once for the `api/v1` surface, and the test meant to make omission impossible enumerates the controllers literally (spec lines 64-71). Nothing cross-checks that list against `ApiV1Module`'s `controllers` array (packages/backend/src/api/v1/api-v1.module.ts:28-35), which is what actually determines the routed surface. Attack path: a future v1 controller with a mutating route is added to `api-v1.module.ts` and its author copies the older two-guard `@UseGuards(...)` form — the route then accepts a key minted with `scopes: ['read']` and mutates, while every existing test still passes because the new class is not in the spec's array. This is the 'reads as covered' failure mode the guard's own docstring (api-key-write-scope.guard.ts:21-30) says it exists to eliminate, relocated from the handler to the controller decorator. Deriving the list from `Reflect.getMetadata('controllers', ApiV1Module)`, or binding the guard at module level, would close it.
searchedFor: Grep 'CombinedAuthGuard|ApiKeyAuthGuard' across packages/backend/src (only api/v1 controllers + api-key module)
Glob packages/backend/src/api/v1/*.ts to enumerate every v1 controller file
Read all six controllers to confirm each carries the guard and that no mutating route hides behind @Get
Grep '@All\(|methodOverride|X-HTTP-Method|APP_GUARD' for global/wildcard bindings and verb spoofing
Read api-key-write-scope.guard.spec.ts to see whether the controller list is derived or literal

samples.summary: Write-scope guard fails open when `request.user` is absent, so it depends entirely on guard ordering
samples.evidence: `if (!user?.isApiKey) return true;` treats 'no authenticated principal on the request' as 'not an API key, therefore allowed'. Today `CombinedAuthGuard` is listed first in every `@UseGuards(...)` so `user` is always populated, but the guard asserts nothing about that invariant: reordering to `@UseGuards(ApiKeyWriteScopeGuard, CombinedAuthGuard)`, or mounting it on a controller without an auth guard, silently turns it into a no-op and a read-scoped key regains write access to that controller. Fail-closed (throw when `user` is undefined on a mutating request, or require `user.isApiKey === false` explicitly) would make it safe independent of ordering. Impact today is nil, hence minor.

samples.summary: PUT /content block validators recurse without a depth bound through table-cell nesting, while the sibling element walk is depth-capped
samples.evidence: `assertValidBlock` recurses into `tableData.rows[r].cells[c].blocks[cb]` with no depth parameter, and on the slides arm `assertValidSlideBlocks` -> `assertValidTextBodyBlocks(cell, ...)` -> `assertValidSlideBlocks` is likewise unbounded. The same commit adds `MAX_ELEMENT_DEPTH = 32` for `data.children` with the explicit reasoning that 'the JSON body limit is 25 MB — enough for a compact payload to exhaust the stack on an authenticated endpoint' (docs-content.controller.ts:611-617), and `JSON_BODY_LIMIT` is indeed '25mb' (packages/backend/src/main.ts:20). A ~60-byte-per-level payload (`{"type":"table","style":{},"tableData":{"rows":[{"cells":[{"blocks":[`) nests hundreds of thousands of levels inside that limit, so any workspace member or write-scoped key can drive the validator into a RangeError on every request. Medium confidence: the RangeError is caught by Nest's exception layer (500 storm, not a process crash) and V8's JSON.parse may reject the depth first — I did not establish empirically which limit binds.

samples.summary: `MIME_TO_EXT[mime]` is an untrusted-key object-literal lookup on the export path — the same defect class this change sweeps to `Map` everywhere else
samples.evidence: `deriveExt` does `MIME_TO_EXT[blob.type.toLowerCase()] || 'bin'`, and the resulting `ext` flows into both a zip entry name (`zip.file(`word/${path}`, blob)`, line 442) and an unescaped XML attribute (`Target="${e.path}"` in document.xml.rels, line 132). This change converts `ROLE_TO_SCHEME`, `LAYOUT_ID_MIGRATIONS`, `DASH_VAL`, `ALGN`, `TYPE_TO_TAG` etc. to `Map` precisely because a prototype key resolves through `Object.prototype`; this sink in the same swept export path was missed. Exploitability is limited: `blob.type` comes from `res.blob()` (packages/cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts:55) and a Content-Type without a '/' parses to '', so reaching `constructor`/`toString` needs a caller-supplied fetcher that sets the Blob type itself, and `Function.prototype.toString` output contains no '"' or '<', so it corrupts the file rather than injecting an attribute. Hence low confidence.

samples.summary: Image `src` is accepted verbatim by the content PUT validator and later fetched with any scheme/host by the export fetcher (SSRF on the exporting client)
samples.evidence: The new PUT contract documents that values inside repaired collections — explicitly including 'an image `src`' (docs/design/rest-api.md) — are stored as given, and nothing in `docs-content.controller.ts` constrains `inline.style.image.src`. `resolveImageUrl` passes through anything matching /^[a-z][a-z0-9+.-]*:/i untouched (image-fetcher.ts:28) and `createImageFetcher` fetches it with no allowlist (line 49). A write-scoped key or any workspace member can plant `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/...` or an internal host in a document; when another user exports it via the CLI, their host fetches the internal resource and embeds the bytes into the exported DOCX/PDF — a read-back exfiltration channel. Pre-existing and outside the diff's edited lines, and I did not verify that any deployment places the CLI where internal endpoints are reachable, hence low confidence.
searchedFor: Grep 'imageFetcher|DocxExporter.export' across the repo for fetcher call sites
Grep the PUT validator in docs-content.controller.ts for any `src` / URL validation (none found)

verdict.reason: The absence is factually real — nothing derives the controller list from ApiV1Module metadata (Reflect.getMetadata appears only once repo-wide, at api-key-write-scope.guard.spec.ts:73, reading __guards__ not controllers; app.module.ts:123 binds only ThrottlerGuard as APP_GUARD; eslint.arch.config.mjs contains only no-restricted-imports rules; no e2e spec exercises scopes) — but it is not a blocking security defect in this tree. All six routed v1 controllers currently carry @UseGuards(CombinedAuthGuard, WorkspaceScopeGuard, ApiKeyWriteScopeGuard) (documents:26, tabs:21, cells:29, docs-content:75, images:24-25, files:49-50), api-v1.module.ts:28-35 registers exactly those six, and a full @Controller( enumeration across src shows no other controller mounts an api/v1 path. The guard is HTTP-method-keyed (api-key-write-scope.guard.ts:38-49), so any new mutating route on an existing controller is gated automatically. No read-scoped API key can reach any mutating v1 route today; the described exposure requires future code that does not exist. The substance of the finding is that a test uses a literal it.each list (spec:64-71) rather than deriving it from module metadata — regression-proofing / test design, explicitly outside this lens ("test quality", "design/architecture fit"). It is a valid hardening suggestion, not an authorization gap or a bypassable gate.
